https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-conten.text: Cancer claims 10 million lives each year, the global shortage of health workers runs into the millions, and in some parts of the world, a single mosquito bite can be fatal. These challenges may seem very different. Yet they share a common element in how many health systems operate: risk is often recognised only after it has become illness, outbreak or crisis. By then, a disease may have advanced, transmission of disease may be under way, or an already stretched workforce may be managing consequences that earlier action could have reduced. The opportunity is to move that point of intervention earlier. This is what anticipatory health means in practice: using signals that already exist, at the bedside, in communities, and in routine health data, to help people and health systems act sooner. It is not prediction for its own sake. The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response. Advertisement Finding practical routes to earlier action That principle sits at the heart of the Future Health Impact Challenge: Building Anticipatory Health Systems through Population Sensing, launched by Future Health – A Global Initiative by Abu Dhabi in collaboration with MIT Solve. The Challenge received 393 submissions from 68 countries. ThinkMD, VectorCam and Huna emerged as its three award-winning solutions: ThinkMD received the grand prize, with VectorCam and Huna recognised as distinguished finalists. Future Health Impact Challenge: Trailer The Challenge was designed to identify practical solutions with evidence of impact and potential to scale. Each of the three selected teams demonstrated their approach to using technology to turn an early signal into decisions that support anticipatory actions a health system can take. Frontline care as a population signal ThinkMD starts with the interaction between a frontline health worker and a patient. Its offline mobile platform guides structured assessments aligned with clinical protocols, supporting providers where doctors, connectivity, and diagnostic tools may be scarce. Almost 10,000 frontline health workers across 885 facilities are now using it. Each consultation also creates structured data. Across facilities, that information can reveal changes in symptoms and service demand. In Zambia, analysis of around one million encounters identified symptom patterns several months before a confirmed cholera outbreak. In Kenya, deployment data showed improvements in identifying danger signs in infants and prescribing antibiotics correctly for childhood pneumonia. Advertisement It is not prediction for its own sake. “The utilisation of AI in healthcare is an absolute game changer. Not only can we increase access for patients, but we can also increase access to information to make correct and appropriate diagnoses and give the right treatment to the right patient at the right time. Future Health has been a really critical platform to be able to accelerate our mission of moving from reactionary to anticipatory care,” said Dr Jackie Rabec of ThinkMD. The award has given ThinkMD support and visibility as it works to expand into new health systems and strengthen how frontline data becomes timely intelligence for decision-makers. That is one measure of the Challenge’s impact: helping proven solutions move towards sustained, wider adoption. Earlier signals from the environment and routine data VectorCam begins with the environment around a community. Using a low-cost smartphone imaging device and offline AI, community health workers can photograph and identify mosquitoes in the field. Each observation generates time- and location-based data that can help authorities see changing vector risk as the first signal of disease patterns, before a spread in local communities and populations. The value lies in connecting early and everyday signals to a timely, practical response. Field evaluations show data completeness rising from approximately 60% to more than 90%. With support from the Future Health Impact Challenge, VectorCam aims to strengthen its early-warning capability, integrate additional data sources and expand into national surveillance programmes. Huna looks for earlier cancer-risk signals in information that health systems already generate. Its platform analyses routine complete blood count data to identify people with an elevated risk and prioritises them for screening. It does not diagnose cancer from a blood test; it helps direct limited screening capacity, and supports patients and healthcare professionals through the next steps. Advertisement In Brazil, Huna’s deployments have screened more than 500,000 people and detected hundreds of cancer cases. Its experience also highlights a critical ‘last mile’: identifying risk is not enough if a person does not complete the diagnostic pathway. Recognition and funding from the Challenge could help support further validation across new populations and facilitate new international partnerships. Innovation is only the starting point Together, these solutions show that useful signals can come from a variety of sources – including clinical encounters, environmental surveillance, and routine diagnostics. They also show that anticipatory approaches can be built where connectivity, specialist capacity, or access to screening is limited, and that innovation developed in those settings can share insights that can be localised and adopted globally. But a successful technology or pilot is not the same as system-wide impact. Scaling requires local validation, integrated into existing workflows, responsible data governance, sustainable financing, workforce training, and evidence that earlier insight changes decisions and outcomes. A successful technology or pilot is not the same as system-wide impact. “The solutions emerging from this Challenge reflect both the urgency and the opportunity facing health systems globally. By bringing innovators together with policymakers, funders and implementers through platforms such as Future Health, we can help accelerate solutions that are locally grounded and capable of delivering impact at scale,” said Hala Hanna, Executive Director of MIT Solve. From recognition to system-level impact Advertisement The Future Health Impact Challenge is part of Future Health’s wider role as a year-round platform for action. Together with our partners and colleagues across diverse sectors and geographies, Future Health identifies promising solutions, supports their development, builds international connections and brings together the policy, clinical, research and investment expertise needed to move from proof to concept to measurable impact. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/19/hegs.text: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth arrived at a military airbase in Bogotá on Wednesday for talks on security cooperation, following an unannounced stopover in Venezuela.Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora received Hegseth at the airbase in the country's capital. Mora had told Congress the previous day that the Pentagon chief would hand over a C-130 Hercules military aircraft during the visit.Hegseth standing alongside Colombian ministers, "In each country, according to each country's laws, but in working together, we are going to find, we are going to hunt, we are going to kill and defeat narcoterrorists." "He added that "each country wants to deny safe haven to those cartels while respecting the sovereignty, the laws and the constitution and the congress of each individual country, but bonding and working together to take a fight to a common enemy in way that has never happened before."Following a closed-door meeting with Hegseth, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula said the government will ask Congress to approve joint military operations with the US. Washington has already supported counter-narcotics strikes inside Colombia.Bula said President Abelardo De la Espriella “has been very clear about his country’s sovereign position, and it is also very clear to the secretary of war after the conversation we had.”Washington and Bogota, allies in the drug warHegseth's visit follows an impeachment attempt in Congress that left him fighting to keep his job less than two years into his tenure.Thomas Massie, a Republican lawmaker critical of Trump, accused him of mismanaging the war with Iran, overstepping his authority in personnel decisions, and carrying out extrajudicial killings through strikes on boats accused of smuggling drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific. Hegseth has survived the push for now.Colombia has traditionally been one of the US' closest allies in the region and Washington and Bogotá have long worked together against drug trafficking, linking the world’s largest cocaine market with one of its biggest producers.Colombia’s new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office in August vowing to confront the country’s many trafficking groups, has since stepped up military cooperation with the US and intensified the crackdown.The top US military officer, General Dan Caine, visited Colombia last week to coordinate joint efforts against drug trafficking. The two countries are carrying out a major offensive against criminal gangs that Washington classifies as terrorist organisations.More than 300 US soldiers recently trained with 400 Colombian troops in anti-trafficking exercises, which US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said highlight “the deep and enduring security partnership between the United States and Colombia.”Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited in September and pledged to “restore” ties with Bogotá after four years of leftist government.Hegseth’s trip comes after Vice President JD Vance cancelled a planned visit to Colombia this month.“The one who’s coming is not Vice President Vance. The one coming is the secretary of war. Tomorrow, I’m going to meet with him,” Mora said on Tuesday. He added that the talks would cover how the US should keep supporting Colombia in “restoring security for Colombians.”One expected topic is Colombia’s participation in the Shield of the Americas, President Donald Trump’s anti-drug alliance, which is backed by about 20 countries.US troops have also carried out joint operations against trafficking and violence in other Latin American countries, including Mexico and Ecuador.
